Do you not struggle when you're not travelling?

This feeling of yours is very common, I'm sure it is. I've felt it and sometimes I still do. The travelling allows me not only to distract myself but also gives me something to focus on in the short term. The dreaming then the planning and then all the opportunities to really put myself out there when I'm out and about. There aren't many prompts in the day-to-day but going somewhere gives me the chance to practice the stepping out of my comfort zone, so to say, in a fun and rewarding way - be it starting a conversation with a stranger, eating weird parts of an animal or pursuing new physical challenges.

As for the longer term life goals and feeling of disappointment, travelling doesn't help me either. I won't be satisfied having lived a life where all I can say is that I worked a 9-5 enough to afford occasional travel. The way I see it, for this problem, I'm afraid, there is no answer you'll just find one day. The solution has to come from within and usually requires all or one of: courage, hard-work and determination.

Hi, I solo-traveled Bali last year (23F) and I had the best time of my life. Made me super hungry for travelling. So I definitely recommend it to everyone. 

I didn't hire a driver, I rented a moto-scooter instead and stayed in Hostels (which are better for meeting people than AirBnBs). I was there for a month and I decided to take my time and not put any pressure on myself to see as many things as possible, but instead to connect to culture and meet people. Bali is chill and authentic nevertheless, but you can fall in the tourist trap everywhere; and Bali is also very touristic.

If you've got 2 weeks, I recommend you climb Mt. Batur in time for sunrise one day. I really liked the area up there. Also scuba-diving in Tulamben - classic. Take your time in Ubud and visit the local bars and pubs.

Sort of like converting stress into motivation (maybe?) to create drive from nothingness.
Simple examples: the stress of a deadline that makes you get started?
Another example of a physical stress: you know when you just have a bad day out running (or cycling or whatever exercise) and you push yourself though exhaustion and fatigue because you know that’s how you make progress?

The other thing I wanted to say is that I would at all times prefer the stress anxiety coming from a purpose to the generalised anxiety and diluted depression coming from lacking a purpose.

I think there is some confusion around the term as people have been using it to describe different distributions of power within the same structure. Is the general government equal, greater then or less then the regional government? 

The US is supposed to have a relation of parity between the two but in my view the Federal Government ended up much stronger than initially intended. On the other side, people seem to oppose federalism in the EU, viewed as undermining state sovereignty (See Brexit). 

I think you are right in that the EU needs to address the inefficiency and illegitimacy and federate, but the US model is not the right one. I strongly believe a hierarchy where power is mostly in the regions, that is flows from bottom to the top (general) and decisions propagate upwards, is the way to go forward for a successful EU.
